finding.claim: The avatar endpoint fetches an arbitrary attacker-supplied URL server-side. The only check is that the URL starts with https://. It does not restrict the host, resolved IP, port or redirects. An attacker can target internal HTTPS services or hostnames that resolve to internal or link-local IPs, such as https://users.internal or a DNS name pointing at 127.0.0.1 or 169.254.169.254. axios follows redirects by default, so an attacker-controlled HTTPS server can also redirect the request to http:// internal targets. The https:// prefix check is bypassed by the redirect. The response is not returned, but the byte length is. That gives a blind SSRF with an oracle for reachability and response size, and it allows internal requests to be triggered.

trace.note: only checks typeof string and startsWith('https://')
axios.get(url) is called with the user URL and default redirect following
response size is returned to the caller

finding.guards_checked: Checked for a scheme prefix check (https:// only), which is present but insufficient. No hostname allowlist, no private, loopback or link-local IP blocking, no DNS resolution or pinning, and no maxRedirects:0. No authentication middleware is present. Express JSON parsing does not validate the URL.

verdict.guard_found: Only a typeof string check and url.startsWith("https://") at server.js:11 (scheme prefix check, not a closing guard); no host allowlist, IP blocking, or maxRedirects limit; no auth middleware.
verdict.reason: server.js:10 takes req.body.avatarUrl from an unauthenticated JSON body, and only a startsWith("https://") check at server.js:11 guards it before axios.get(url) at server.js:14, with the byte length returned at server.js:15, so a blind SSRF is reachable.
